New Research Published by IMF: Causes and Consequences of Income Inequality: A Global Perspective. Well Worth the Time to Read Through

Better access to education (as captured by declining educational inequality), improved health outcomes, and redistributive social polices help raise the income share of the poor and the middle class irrespective of the level of economic development of a country.17 By contrast, easing of labor market regulations and technological progress dampen the income share of the poor and the middle class, consistent with other studies

This in-depth global study pokes massive holes in the purported lie that trickle-down economics is beneficial for economic growth. Rather, it is the opposite. "the benefits do not trickle down" -- "When the top earners in society make more money, it actually slows down economic growth. On the other hand, when poorer people earn more, society as a whole benefits."

Economic globalization is the best way to take down poverty in undeveloped/developing countries. The Brookings Institute (Chandy and Gertz) did a study reporting that between 2005 and 2015, the number of people experiencing "extreme poverty" (as defined by the IMF and World Bank as 1.25 USD per day) has dropped from 1.3 billion people in 2005 to 600 million in 2015. They also proved this to be 84% due to economic globalization by showing that countries with open borders since 2005 experienced 6% economic growth per year (except in 2009) while countries with closed borders only experienced 1% growth per year.

Globalization has a side-effect I never find anyone talking about. America's failing infrastructure, in terms of manufacturing and related, is a direct result of globalization. The money and social systems flee from the top countries and (ironically) trickle to the countries with the least worker rights and most corporate protectionism.

This has happened repeatedly in history, Thatcherism in the UK was the consequence as the UK suffered massive migrant worker influxes after WW2. These migrant influxes resulted in all the social systems in the UK collapsing, as businesses could fire whole unions of workers and hire immigrants. These same caveats apply to immigration policies, and why certain jobs in the U.S. are still so badly paid. Immigrants do in fact not only "take jobs", but reduce the earning potential of a job by being willing to do things others will not unless better paid.

A countries infrastructure and internal welfare depends heavily on ensuring protectionism of certain sectors (manufacturing), as well as strictly controlling immigration to prevent migrants from devaluing jobs by ignorance. Ignorance, for example, of realizing being paid $7 to do a horrible job nobody else wants to do hurts their earning potential considerably.

These problems absolutely need to be considered where globalization and immigration is concerned. It can ruin a country, as it did to the UK, if allowed to go without proper control.

Finally: While GDP may increase from globalization, that increase is exclusively in the uppermost classes. Meanwhile, lower classes become devalued. That latter correlation is conveniently never brought up.
Yeah that's the ironic problem. Developed countries initiate globalization and it hurts them, while the undeveloped countries benefit.

I certainly would put restrictions on it. I approve of investing in foreign countries for its economic benefits, but only so far as it does not hurt us.

The same is true of immigration. Only allow immigration of those who are fluent in our culture and language, which is very easily achieved thanks to the internet and the near universal teaching of English in foreign countries. Yet I find myself working with people who only speak Spanish, and refuse to learn any English - a circumstance that should not be allowed. Due to how poor these people tend to be, I believe this can be rectified by free access to education, especially to the poor. For immigrants, a time-cap of fluency or continued progress within a certain number of years seems acceptable if access is free.

Hell, just recommending them Duolingo would work.
